Stage 3 · Grammar

If this happens, that will happen

The sentence you need for anything that is real and still possible.

Read these four sentences. They all come from the text later in this lesson.
  • If the flu season is bad, offices will go back to the elbow bump.
  • If you meet a client in Germany, you will probably still shake hands.
  • If you get it wrong, nobody will be angry.
  • The first impression might be strange if you use the wrong greeting.
What tense comes after if?
The two halves
The if clause — the conditionThe result clauseWatch out
If the flu season is bad,offices will go back to the elbow bump.present + will
If you get it wrong,nobody will be angry.will + base form, no to
If you don’t wash your hands,you won’t stop the germs.either half can be negative
If you use the wrong greeting,the impression might be strange.might = less certain than will
If the hand comes forward,take it.an order can be the result
Offices will go back to the elbow bumpif the flu season is bad.reversed — and now no comma
Put the halves in the right order to build the rule.

WHAT IT DOES. It talks about a real, possible future. If it rains, we will stay inside — rain is genuinely possible today.

FORM. if + Present Simple, then will / won’t / might + base form. Both halves can be negative.

ORDER. Either half can come first. Comma only when if starts the sentence.

Not “If it will rain”. The future goes in the other half, never after if.

LOOKING AHEAD. If I were you… is a different sentence for imaginary things. That is Unit 11 — not now.

WHAT IT DOES. This sentence links a real condition to its real result. Use it when the thing in the if half may well happen: If the shop is open, I will buy some bread. The shop may be open — that is the point.

FORM. if + Present Simple + will / won’t / might + base form. The verb after if looks like the present, but the meaning is future. English does this on purpose: one future marker per sentence is enough.

WILL OR MIGHT. will = you are sure of the result. might = it is one possible result of several. If I finish early, I will call you / If I finish early, I might call you.

ORDER AND COMMA. If you come late, we will start without you. = We will start without you if you come late. Same meaning. The comma appears only in the first version.

Three mistakes to watch: “If it will rain” (future after if) · “If it rains, we stay inside” (missing will) · “If it rains, we will to stay” (extra to).

LOOKING AHEAD. Lesson 26 keeps the same present tense but swaps if for when, as soon as and until. The tense rule does not change.

Five sentences from the text. Read each one and find the two verbs.

Full grammar reference — The first conditional

Form

StructureIf + Present Simple, will + plain verb
ExampleIf you greet people warmly, they will remember you.
Order can changeThey will remember you if you greet them warmly. (no comma)
NegativeIf it doesn’t rain, we won’t cancel.
Other results… we might go · … you should ask · … call me. (imperative)

Spelling and sound

Write a comma when the if clause comes first; no comma when it comes second.

When and why we use it

  • The first conditional talks about a real, possible future situation and its result.
  • The if clause uses a present form even though it refers to the future.
  • Might in the result clause makes it less certain: If it rains, we might stay in.
  • Unless means ‘if not’: Unless you book, you won’t get a place.

Signal words

if · unless · in case · then

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • If it will rain, we’ll stay in. → If it rains, we’ll stay in.No will after if.
  • If you will ask, he will help. → If you ask, he will help.Same rule.
  • If I see her I’ll tell her. → If I see her, I’ll tell her.Comma when if comes first.
  • If you don’t hurry, you will late. → … you will be late.Will needs a verb.

Don’t confuse it with

First conditional = real and possible. Second conditional (Unit 11) = imaginary. If it rains… against If it snowed in July…

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Where the handshake came from, and what is happening to it now.

Before you read: the handshake is about five hundred years old in Europe. Why do you think it started?

Choose one. The text gives one popular answer — see if it is yours.

1 · Read the text once. Match a heading to each paragraph.

One minute. Do not write anything else yet.

The rise and fall of the handshake

A  Nobody knows exactly when people started to shake hands. One popular idea is that an open hand showed you carried no weapon, so the handshake began as a sign of trust and respect. For hundreds of years it was the safest greeting in business: firm, short, the same for everyone.

B  Then, in 2020, the world stopped touching. Doctors explained that a single handshake can move germs from one palm to another in a second, and that a virus travels fastest between people who greet each other all day. Offices put up notices: you must wash your hands, and you don’t have to shake hands with anyone.

C  Five years later, the handshake has not disappeared, but it now shares the job with other greetings. In many places a nod, a smile or a fist bump has taken its place. Some people think this trend is ridiculous. Others say it is simply more informal — and more honest.

D  So what happens next? If the flu season is bad, offices will go back to the elbow bump. If you meet a client in Germany, you will probably still shake hands. If you get it wrong, nobody will be angry — but the first impression might be strange. And if you are not sure what to do, watch the other person’s hand: if it comes forward, take it.

E  Perhaps the real rule is older than the handshake. If you greet people warmly, they will remember you. The hand is only the messenger.

Sources. Written for this course from public-health reporting on greetings and hand hygiene from 2020 onwards, and from the standard account of the handshake as a gesture that showed an empty hand. The offices, the notices and the individual examples are invented.
